subject: Accounting
title: FTX and Missing Billions
description: One-minute skill: FTX and Missing Billions.

hook.text: Crypto exchange FTX had no proper accounting department. Billions of dollars went missing.

buildup.text: Sam Bankman-Fried built a $32 billion empire with no audited financial statements.

discovery.text: Customer funds were secretly lent to his trading firm Alameda Research.

twist.text: FTX used QuickBooks—small business software—to track billions. Audits were from unknown firms.

climax.text: FTX collapsed in days. Bankman-Fried was convicted of fraud and sentenced to 25 years.

quiz.question: What basic accounting failure defined FTX?
options: No proper accounting department or audited statements

details.summary: FTX was a cryptocurrency exchange that collapsed in 2022 when it was revealed that customer funds had been diverted to a sister trading firm. This topic covers the complete absence of financial controls, the role of Sam Bankman-Fried, and lessons for digital asset regulation.
details.whyItMatters: FTX showed that even in modern fintech, basic accounting controls matter. The absence of proper bookkeeping, auditing, and governance enabled billions in customer funds to vanish.
takeaways: FTX commingled customer deposits with its trading arm Alameda Research without disclosure
The company had no proper accounting department and tracked finances partly in spreadsheets and Slack
Sam Bankman-Fried was convicted of fraud and sentenced to 25 years in prison

faq.question: What happened at FTX?
faq.answer: FTX, a major cryptocurrency exchange, secretly transferred billions in customer deposits to its affiliated trading firm Alameda Research, which lost the money on risky trades. When a bank run exposed the shortfall in November 2022, FTX collapsed within days.

faq.question: How did FTX operate without basic accounting controls?
faq.answer: FTX had no CFO for most of its existence, lacked a proper accounting department, used QuickBooks (meant for small businesses) for a multi-billion-dollar company, commingled funds freely, and had almost no independent board oversight. It was a governance vacuum.
